title: Highly Selective Methane Production Through Electrochemical CO2 reduction by Electrolytically Plated Cu-Co Electrode
abstract: Among the electrode materials used for electrolytic CO2 reduction, only Cu shows a special function of producing not only carbon monoxide (CO), but also hydrocarbons from CO2. We found that, in electrolytic CO2 reduction using an electrolytically plated Cu-Co electrode, a hydrocarbon product with high faradaic efficiency (FE) could be obtained with low-FE CO. The plated electrodes have a Co solid solution on the Cu surface. The non-localized Co changes the adsorption energy of the reaction intermediate in CO2 reduction. Consequently, by increasing the Co content in Cu, HCOOH can be selectively produced. Further, in electrolytic CO2 reduction with an applied potential of − 1.19 V vs. reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE), the selectivity of methane (CH4) production improved, while the selectivity of ethylene (C2H4) formation lowered. In the reduction using the plated electrode containing 14% Co, the FE of CH4 production reached the highest at 47.7%. These results suggested that mixing Co in Cu promotes the hydrogenation of CH2 * to CH3 * and inhibits the dimerization of CH2 * species. Furthermore, this research on plated electrodes is useful for the development of catalytic electrodes for electrolytic CO2 reduction.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text:
The rise in CO2 emissions caused by fossil fuel consumption is a significant global problem because increasing CO2 emissions cause greenhouse effect and damage the environment [1]. Many approaches, such as chemical, biological, and inorganic approaches, have been explored to resolve this problem. Although CO2 fixation, emission control, and conversion technologies are challenging strategies, they are required to prevent global warming [2–4]. Among these technologies, CO2 conversion can produce useful substances of industrial source such as CO, CH4, C2H4, and HCOOH. The
electrochemical reduction of CO2 employing various metals has the possibility of CO2 fixation and conversion by utilizing renewable energy sources for a sustainable society. Electrochemical CO2 reduction by various metals has been researched exhaustively and its main product varies based on the metal species of the electrode in the case of aqueous solution [5]. Au, Ag, Zn, and Pb electrodes produce CO as the main product by electrochemical reduction of CO2, whereas Sn, Hg, and Pb electrodes produce HCOOH under the same condition of electrochemical CO2 reduction. On the other hand, hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) preferentially occurs in case of Fe, Ni, Co, Ti, and Pt. Among the metal species, copper produce unique main products during electrochemical CO2 reduction, that is, hydrocarbons [6–8]. The product selectivity is considered to be related to the adsorption energy between the metal surface and CO2 and intermediates such as *CO and *COOH. Alloying is one of the approaches to control the adsorption energy and product selectivity of electrochemical CO2 reduction. We previously reported electrochemical CO2 reduction employing a Cu-Sn electrode that was prepared by electroplating [9]. In the report, * Tetsuya Haruyama haruyama@life.kyutech.ac.jp 1 Division of Functional Interface Engineering, Department of Biological Functions and Engineering, Kyushu Institute of Technology, Kitakyushu Science and Research Park, Kitakyushu, Fukuoka 808-0196, Japan
2 Advanced Catalytic Transformation Program for Carbon Utilization (ACT-C), Japan Science and Technology Agency (JST), Tokyo 102-0076, Japan
we indicated the possibility of controlling the CO2 reduction product as CO or HCOO− by the composition of the Cu-Sn electrode and discussed CO2 adsorption on the respective electrodes. However, it is difficult to control hydrocarbon productions characterizing copper electrode. Recently, a Cu catalyst for CO2 reduction has been researched to control Cu nanostructures [10–12]. Similarly, oxide-derived Cu was reported to have a high selectivity toward C2H4 during CO2 reduction [13, 14]. On the other hand, the development of computational science such as density functional theory (DFT) calculations indicated that hydrocarbon production depends on the binding energy of the intermediate product CO to the electrode [8]. Moreover, the reaction pathway for product selectivity of electrochemical CO2 reduction was discussed by DFT calculations [15–18]. For hydrocarbon selectivity in CO2 reduction, various Cu-based alloys were researched such as CuZn, Cu-Au, and Cu-Co. Cu-Au and Cu-Zn were reported to produce alcohols by CO2 reduction [19, 20]. Grote et al. reported that generation of C2 species increased during CO2 reduction using a Cu-Co electrode (Co content is 5–15 at%) [21]. On the other hand, the Cu-Co alloy electrode prepared by us through electroplating increased the selectivity toward CH4 among hydrocarbons during CO2 reduction. In this study, we report and discuss the selectivity of hydrocarbons by CO2 reduction on our Cu-Co electrode.

sections.heading: Preparation of Cu-Co Electrode
sections.text: For pretreatment, a Cu plate (Nilaco) with a thickness of 2 mm was ultrasonicated three times at 28 kHz in ultrapure water for 5 min. The ultrasonicated Cu plate was immersed in 1 M HCl for 30 s, rinsed with ultrapure water, and dried in a N2 atmosphere. Cu-Co electrodes were prepared by electrodeposition, wherein the bath consisted of 0.5 M potassium pyrophosphate (Sigma-Aldrich) and 0.2 M potassium bitartrate (SigmaAldrich), and the total metal ion concentration was controlled to 0.2 M using CuSO4·6H2O (Wako) and CoSO4·5H2O (Wako). To prepare the Cu-Co electrode, electroplating was performed with a two-electrode system using a potentiostat/ galvanostat (HOKUTO DENKO, HZ 7000) with the pretreated Cu plate and a Pt plate as the working and counter electrodes, respectively. The metal ion concentrations of the electroplating baths and operating current densities are shown in Table 1. The electroplating operation time was 5 min.

sections.heading: Cu-Co Electrode Characterization
sections.text:
Scanning electronmicroscope (SEM) images were obtained at 15 kV using a JSM-6701 SEM (JEOL), and the ion
concentrations of the prepared electrodes were determined by energy-dispersive X-ray spectrometry (EDS). The thin filmXray diffraction (XRD) profiles of the Cu-Co electrodes were obtained using an X-ray diffractometer (MAC science, MO3XHF22) in the 2θ rage from 30° to 80°. The composition of the prepared Cu-Co electrode was analyzed by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, Shimadzu, KRATOS AXISNOVA) using Al Kα as the X-ray source.

sections.heading: CO2 Electroreduction
sections.text:
Electrochemical CO2 reduction was performed using a three-electrode system and an H-type cell, in which the
cathode and anode cells were separated by an ionexchange membrane (Sigma-Aldrich, Nafion NRE-212). In the three-electrode system, the working, counter, and reference electrodes were the Cu-Co electrode, Pt plate, and Ag/AgCl in saturated KCl, respectively. The electrolyte which is both the anolyte and catholyte used in the CO2 reduction experiment was 0.1 M potassium bicarbonate (Wako) saturated with CO2 (99.995%) by bubbling for 40 min. In the catholyte, CO2 concentration was saturated as 34 mM. In the CO2 reduction experiment, CO2 gas at a flow rate of 5 mL/min was continuously supplied. In the electrochemical measurements, the potentiostat/galvanostat (HOKUTO DENKO, HZ 7000) controlled the applied potential collected by IR drop and measured the current. The applied potentials of the Ag/AgCl electrode in saturated KCl with reference to a reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) were − 0.89 to − 1.19 V vs. RHE for 30 min.

sections.heading: Analysis of CO2 Reduction Product
sections.text: The gas-phase CO2 reduction product was collected in a gas bag (GL Sciences, Smart bag PA) and analyzed by gas chromatography (GC, Shimadzu, Tracera (GC-2010 Plus A, BID-2010 Plus)) with a GC column (Shinwa Chemical Industries, Micropacked ST) and He carrier gas (purity no less than 99.999%). For analysis of formic acid, the liquid phase of the CO2 reduction product was analyzed by anion chromatography (Shimadzu, Prominence HIC-SP) with a Shim-pack IC-SA3 column (Shimadzu) and 3.6 mM sodium carbonate (Wako) as the eluting solvent. Faraday efficiency (FE) was calculated from the amount of reduction products and the measurement of electric quantity.

sections.heading: Characterization of Cu-Co Electrodes
sections.text:
Bimetallic Cu-Co electrodes and monometallic Cu and Co electrodes were prepared by electrodeposition under various applied potential conditions, as shown in Table 1. The morphologies of the prepared electrodes were characterized by SEM, and the elemental composition of each prepared electrode was analyzed by EDS (Fig. 1). In Fig. 1, the Cu/Co atomic ratio is shown in the top-left corner of the SEM images and the preparation ratio (Cu/Co) is shown in brackets. The Cu/Co atomic ratio differs from the preparation ratio because Co is more electronegative than Cu. Moreover, the SEM images of the electrodes show that the morphologies changed with increasing Co content. The electrodeposited Cu electrode (Cu100) shows large grain aggregates, whereas the electrodeposited Co electrode (Co100) shows needle-like crystals (data not shown). The grain aggregates of the Cu-Co electrodes tend to become smaller and finer with increasing Co content.
Figure 2 shows the XRD profiles of the prepared electrodes. The Cu-Co electrodes show neither peak shift nor broad peaks
corresponding to Cu despite the presence of Co, as detected by EDS. These results suggested that Co is solid soluted in the Cu crystalline framework, i.e., formed a substitutional solid solution. Figure 3 shows the XPS spectra of the electrodes. The binding energies of Cu 2p in all the electrodes are similar and show no change in spite of Co inclusion. The binding energy of Co 2p was observed with increasing Co content.

sections.heading: CO2 Reduction
sections.text:
Electrochemical CO2 reduction was performed using an Htype cell in which the anode and cathode sections were separated by a cation-exchange membrane [9]. The applied potential was − 0.89 V to − 1.19 V vs RHE for 30 min, and the FE of the CO2 reduction product was calculated from the amount of CO2 reduction product and electrical quantity for different applied potentials (Fig. 4). At − 0.89 V vs. RHE, HER is the preferential reaction and formic acid is the main product of CO2 reduction reaction. The presence of Co did not affect the selectivity of CO2 reduction reaction including HER. On the other hand, the CH4 selectivity of CO2 reduction increased with Co content, and the maximum CH4 selectivity was
47.7% for 14% Co content; meanwhile, the C2H4 selectivity of CO2 reduction decreased. The CH4 selectivity of CO2 reduction decreased for 22.5% Co content. These results partially agree with the research of Grote et al. [21]. They insisted that a low Co content (5–15%) increased C2 selectivity of CO2 reduction at − 1.2 V vs. RHE. Our result is consistent with the change in selectivity of hydrocarbons with Co content (0– 20%). However, in our research, the selectivity of C1 product, i.e., CH4, increased, while the C2 selectivity of CO2 reduction decreased, which is contrary to their assertion. Nie et al. [17] reported that ethylene formation, i.e., dimerization of two CH2
* species, is a non-electrochemical step. Moreover, they insisted that the hydrogenation of CH2 * to CH3 * requires an applied potential of − 1.15 vs. RHE on Cu(111) by DFT calculations [17]. The Cu-Co electrode is expected to change the adsorption energy of the intermediate products by the mixing of Co. In our case, it is considered that the hydrogenation of CH2 * to CH3 * is promoted and the dimerization of CH2
* species is inhibited by mixing a small amount of Co. Through DFT calculations, Hirunsit et al. reported that Cu containing Co, i.e., Cu3Co(211), forms a stable COH
* species and promotes HCOOH production [22]. Our results similarly show that HCOOH production increased upon Co mixing.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: Bimetallic Cu-Co electrodes with different low Co contents were prepared by electrodeposition. It was revealed that in the prepared electrodes, Co is present as a solid dispersion in a Cu crystalline framework. In CO2 reduction reaction, the mixing of Co to Cu increased the selectivity of HCOOH production under various applied potential conditions and increased the selectivity of CH4 production at − 1.19 V vs. RHE. The highest FE of the CH4 product reached 47.7% for 14% Co content. This is because the Co content in Cu changed the adsorption energy of the intermediate products. As a result, it is considered that the hydrogenation of CH2 * to CH3 * is promoted and the dimerization of CH2 * species is inhibited. This research can be expected to be useful for the development of electrode catalysts for CO2 reduction.
